article_title: Including Learning Analytics in the Loop of Self-Paced Online Course Learning Design
citation: Hongxin Yan, Fuhua Lin & Kinshuk. (2021). Including Learning Analytics in the Loop of Self-Paced Online Course Learning Design. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education (2021) 31:878–895. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00225-z
title: The Learning Design-Analytic (LDA) model: course learning design and learning analytics mutually support each other in self-paced online learning
description: The LDA model is a proposed model of learning design interacting with learning analytics, suggested mainly for STEM disciplines in self-paced online learning. In it, course learning design builds learning activities which generate learning data; learning analytics uses those data to mitigate SPOL learning barriers, and its results feed back to improve the design. The article states that 'course learning design that aims for learning success builds learning activities, which generate the learning data' and that analytics results 'can, in turn, empower the course learning design by facilitating a data-driven approach.'
requirements: Sufficient and meaningful data-collection points must be embedded in the course by designing certain learning activities, such as check-point activities like quizzes, posting, and reflecting
constraints: The model is suggested mainly for STEM disciplines in self-paced online learning in higher formal education
target_learners: adult learners in self-paced online higher education courses
target_learning_goals: learning success in STEM disciplines, including conceptual development, inquiry-based and problem-solving skills
examples: The COMP272 Data Structures and Algorithms course revision at Athabasca University follows the LDA model by planning a diagnostic test, a learner profile survey, and unit-level formative assessment.
key_sources: Hongxin Yan, Fuhua Lin & Kinshuk. (2021). Including Learning Analytics in the Loop of Self-Paced Online Course Learning Design. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education (2021) 31:878–895. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00225-z

article_title: Effect of low-dose, high-frequency advanced life support training versus annual full-day training on simulation-based resuscitation performance: a randomized controlled trial.
citation: Moll Lisa, Riessen Reimer, Dahlmann Philipp, Häske David. (2026). Effect of low-dose, high-frequency advanced life support training versus annual full-day training on simulation-based resuscitation performance: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09717-3
title: Replace infrequent intensive refresher courses with regular short scenario-based sessions with feedback for maintaining resuscitation competence
description: The article recommends distributing resuscitation training as brief, recurring team scenarios rather than relying on annual intensive courses. Intervention participants trained "every 4 weeks, using a single CPR scenario in accordance with the ALS standard" in sessions of "about 10 to 15 min" ending with brief feedback. The authors argue short sessions "may represent a feasible alternative that integrates into the routine workflow" where time pressure limits extended training, and frame the superiority of the format via constructive alignment of objectives, activities and assessment.
requirements: Sessions must adhere to the ALS standard and conclude with brief feedback from qualified trainers
constraints: Benefits demonstrated only in a simulation-based, single-German-EMS-system, adult out-of-hospital context; translation to real cardiac arrest, in-hospital, pediatric or neonatal settings not established
target_learners: Emergency medical services professionals (paramedics and emergency medical technicians)
target_learning_goals: Maintain advanced life support competence and resuscitation team management skills over time
examples: The intervention group received CPR training every 4 weeks in 10–15 minute scenario sessions with brief feedback, while the control group received one ERC ALS course day
key_sources: Moll Lisa, Riessen Reimer, Dahlmann Philipp, Häske David. (2026). Effect of low-dose, high-frequency advanced life support training versus annual full-day training on simulation-based resuscitation performance: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09717-3

article_title: Effect of low-dose, high-frequency advanced life support training versus annual full-day training on simulation-based resuscitation performance: a randomized controlled trial.
citation: Moll Lisa, Riessen Reimer, Dahlmann Philipp, Häske David. (2026). Effect of low-dose, high-frequency advanced life support training versus annual full-day training on simulation-based resuscitation performance: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09717-3
title: Validated 29-item ALS resuscitation performance rating instrument with blinded expert and supplementary student rating
description: A self-developed rating instrument comprising four categories with 29 items covering technical and non-technical skills, each rated on a 5-point Likert scale (1 = poor, 5 = excellent). Items were refined from exploratory video analyses and reviewed by an interdisciplinary panel of six experts using a semi-structured consensus approach. Reliability was confirmed with "a Cronbach's alpha of 0.793 and an intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.794 (95% confidence interval: 0.718-0.854)". Six blinded expert raters scored every video, and a supplementary blinded assessment by six student raters independently evaluated all 13 video scenarios.
requirements: Ratings are aggregated as mean scores per item from six independent, blinded raters; discrepancies are not resolved by consensus
constraints: Although validated, the instrument is not yet internationally established, and the score is a composite measure of guideline-adherent processes in a simulated setting that cannot be directly translated into patient outcomes
target_learners: Emergency medical services professionals (paramedics and emergency medical technicians)
target_learning_goals: Assess resuscitation management performance, including technical, non-technical and procedural domains
examples: The instrument was used to rate video-recorded standardized simulation scenarios at baseline and 12-month follow-up, with the team leader as the focus of evaluation
key_sources: Moll Lisa, Riessen Reimer, Dahlmann Philipp, Häske David. (2026). Effect of low-dose, high-frequency advanced life support training versus annual full-day training on simulation-based resuscitation performance: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09717-3

article_title: Framing Metrics, Outcomes, and Assessment Overview in Leadership Programs.
citation: Hastings, L. J., and D. Rosch. 2025. "Framing Metrics, Outcomes, and Assessment Overview in Leadership Programs." New Directions for Student Leadership 2025, no. 187: 85–91. https://doi.org/10.1002/yd.70007
title: Leadership development advancements framework mapping research findings to outcome, assessment, and metric considerations
description: The article organizes advancements in leadership development research—complex context-influenced learners, leadership as dynamic process, longitudinal non-linear development, multi-level development, and early lifespan development—into a framework mapping each to outcome, assessment, and metric considerations. It states that "LD is longitudinal, non‐linear, multi‐level (both individual and team levels), happening earlier than we think, and largely influenced by context," challenging program design, metrics, outcomes, and assessment.
requirements: Assessment methods must be intentionally matched to the explicitly stated level of the program outcome
Longitudinal assessment should track an outcome over time with three or more waves of data and a sensible time metric
constraints: LE does not serve its intended purpose well via disconnected short‐term programs devoid of learner context and focused solely on leader development
target_learners: college and university students in leadership education programs
target_learning_goals: leadership learning and leader development across individual and collective levels
key_sources: Hastings, L. J., and D. Rosch. 2025. "Framing Metrics, Outcomes, and Assessment Overview in Leadership Programs." New Directions for Student Leadership 2025, no. 187: 85–91. https://doi.org/10.1002/yd.70007

article_title: Dear admission committee…: Which moves in application essays predict student master grades?
citation: de Boer, Van Rijnsoever, de Bresser. (2024). Dear admission committee…: Which moves in application essays predict student master grades? PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0304394
title: LDA-derived seven-move coding of application essays
description: A text-mining element in which Latent Dirichlet Allocation distills topics from application essays and aggregates them into moves, defined as "a functional unit of text, which has an identifiable purpose". Thirty topics were reduced to seven moves (master specific, research skills, prior education, societal impact, interest to learn, city and university, extracurricular); per-essay move probabilities (0–1) served as predictors of master grades. The approach replaces subjective essay ratings, which suffer poor interrater reliability, with probabilistic topic measures.
requirements: A corpus of application essays processed with stemming, lemmatization and stop-word removal, and a chosen number of topics (30 here) selected via topic-density criteria
constraints: The authors note the unstructured essay format and sheer volume of text make systematic assessment difficult, and essay-based admission may favor students from advantaged socio-economic backgrounds
target_learners: prospective master students in higher education
target_learning_goals: predicting study success for admission decisions
examples: Applied to 820 completed master files from four cohorts (2014–2017) at the Faculty of Geosciences, Utrecht University, across eleven English-taught two-year master programs
key_sources: de Boer, Van Rijnsoever, de Bresser. (2024). Dear admission committee…: Which moves in application essays predict student master grades? PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0304394

article_title: Helping babies breathe: assessing the effectiveness of simulation-based high-frequency recurring training in a community-based setting of Pakistan.
citation: Mubeen Kiran, Baig Marina, Abbas Sadia, Adnan Farzana, Lakhani Arusa, Bhamani Shireen Shehzad, Rehman Bushra, Shahid Shahnaz, Jan Rafat. (2021). Helping babies breathe: assessing the effectiveness of simulation-based high-frequency recurring training in a community-based setting of Pakistan. BMC Pediatrics. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12887-021-03014-2
title: Low Dose High Frequency (LDHF) capacity-building approach
description: LDHF is a capacity-building approach defined in the article as one that promotes maximal retention of clinical knowledge, skills, and attitudes through short, targeted in-service simulation-based learning activities, spaced over time, and reinforced with structured, ongoing practice sessions on the job. This study operationalized it as simulation-based high-frequency recurring HBB workshops with intermittent on-site supervision, adapted for community midwives who could not commute frequently for practice.
requirements: Short, targeted in-service simulation-based learning activities spaced over time
Structured ongoing on-the-job practice sessions or supervised support between sessions
constraints: The article notes applying LDHF in remote settings with community midwives was challenging and highly resource-intensive, motivating the centralized recurring-session adaptation
target_learners: In-service health workers such as community midwives in low-resource settings
target_learning_goals: Retention of clinical knowledge, skills, and attitudes for newborn resuscitation
examples: The study delivered all content in one day followed by two refresher sessions at two-month intervals, with random monthly supervision visits using the Neonatalie Simulator.
key_sources: Mubeen Kiran, Baig Marina, Abbas Sadia, Adnan Farzana, Lakhani Arusa, Bhamani Shireen Shehzad, Rehman Bushra, Shahid Shahnaz, Jan Rafat. (2021). Helping babies breathe: assessing the effectiveness of simulation-based high-frequency recurring training in a community-based setting of Pakistan. BMC Pediatrics. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12887-021-03014-2
